<meta>continues from previous page</meta>then it is an imperfect verb <term>fiʿl muḍāriʿ</term>.

**Preliminary Note:** If a word indicates a past event and does not accept the feminine *tāʾ* suffix <note>original: "al-tāʾ li-thintān"</note>, or if it indicates a second occurrence in the present and future but does not accept *lam*, such as *awwah* <gloss>an interjection of sighing or pain</gloss>, it is also considered a verbal noun. The author stated this in his work *al-ʿUmdah*.

This is the chapter on the inflected <term>al-muʿrab</term> and the uninflected <term>al-mabnī</term>.

The noun is partly flexible <term>mutamakkin</term>, which is the inflected form representing the original default state <note>original: "al-aṣl"</note>. Its other part is non-flexible <term>ghayr mutamakkin</term>, which is the uninflected form, established contrary to the default state.

The noun is made uninflected due to its resemblance to particles <term>shabah al-ḥarf</term>. This relates to his statement that it is uninflected, meaning an explanation for its lack of inflection. Another view was claimed regarding what deviates from the uninflected state, which concerns cases where inflection is required by a counteracting factor, such as *ayy* <gloss>which / whichever</gloss> in interrogation and conditional clauses. For although it resembles the particle in meaning, this resemblance is countered by its obligatory state of annexation <term>iḍāfah</term>.

A single aspect of resemblance to a particle is sufficient to make a noun uninflected. This contrasts with the prohibition of full inflection or nunation <term>manʿ al-ṣarf</term> <gloss>diptote status</gloss>, where resemblance to a verb from two aspects is strictly required. Ibn al-Ḥājib justified this in his *Amālī* by stating that a single resemblance to a particle places the noun into a different genus and brings close that between which and the particle there is no shared affinity, except in the broadest category, which is being a word. By contrast, the resemblance of a noun to a verb, even if it is another distinct class, does not share the same extreme distance from the noun as the particle does.

From the author's restriction of the cause of indeclinability exclusively to resemblance to the particle, it is understood that other factors are not considered. Abū al-Fatḥ <note>Ibn Jinnī</note> and others preceded him in this view, even if it has been said otherwise.

<summary>This page explains the criteria distinguishing verbal nouns, introduces the chapter on inflected and uninflected nouns, and examines the theoretical basis for noun indeclinability through resemblance to particles versus diptote inflection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ibn Rushd’s argument that prophecy is proven by the specific function of the prophet—legislating divine Law—rather than merely by supernatural physical feats. He uses the analogy of a doctor: just as healing proves someone is a physician, establishing a transformative Law through revelation proves someone is a prophet.</meta>

-> ### The Discovery of the Methods of Proof Regarding the Beliefs of the Religion<-

Just as it is understood that one who performs healing is a physician, it is likewise self-evident that the specific activity of the **Prophets** (peace be upon them) is the establishing of **Laws** <term>Laws</term> <note>original: *shara'i'*. The systematic divine codes of conduct and belief.</note> through **revelation** <term>revelation</term> <note>original: *wahy*. The process by which God communicates His word to a human messenger.</note> from God. Thus, anyone who performs this act is a Prophet. As for the first principle <note>The principle that Prophets are defined by the act of legislating through revelation.</note>, the Mighty Book has drawn attention to it in the words of the Almighty: *“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him,”* up to His words, *“and to Moses God spoke directly”* <note>Quran 4:163-164</note>. It is also known through the actions they command and the sciences they point toward, which do not resemble humanly acquired knowledge or practices that are typically learned. This is because a **breaking of the habitual** <term>breaking of the habitual</term> <note>original: *khariq lil-mu'tad*. The technical term for a miracle; something that "tears" the veil of natural habit.</note>, when it occurs within the realm of knowledge through the establishing of Laws, indicates that the establishment of those Laws was not through learning, but rather through revelation from God; this is what is called **prophecy** <term>prophecy</term>. However, a supernatural act that does not exist within the very act of establishing the Law—such as the **splitting of the sea** <note>Reference to the miracle of Moses.</note> and the like—does not necessarily or inherently prove this specific quality <note>i.e., the quality of being a divinely inspired legislator.</note>. <summary>Ibn Rushd argues that prophecy is verified by the Prophet's ability to establish divine laws and reveal unique knowledge, which he considers a more essential "miracle" than physical wonders like splitting the sea. He supports this by citing Quranic verses that emphasize Muhammad's continuity with previous law-giving prophets.</summary>

<keywords>Prophecy, Revelation, Law, Quranic Proofs, Ibn Rushd, Miracles, Legislation, Knowledge</keywords>

Rufinus, and the *Tripartite History* <note>original: "Historia Tripartita"</note> with some variations from the edition of the Maurist Garet. Some variant readings are still found in the DCLX Codex, in which we have several works of Saint Ambrose. The first sixteen books of the *Origins* <note>original: "Origines"</note> by Saint Isidore of Seville are found to be quite different from the printed versions in the LV Codex. But the learned will be even more pleased with the LIII Codex, in which, besides all the books of these *Origins*, there is a book by the same Saint Isidore *de numeris* <gloss>on numbers</gloss>, a book that scholars have deemed lost. The Abbot Rivautella is thinking of producing an edition of it, which will do him no small honor, and will increase the reputation he has already acquired in the world with the two volumes of the Turin Marbles, which he illustrated together with the late, most learned Abbot Ricolvi. Let us come to the tenth century. Only two codices of this century shall be mentioned by us: the DCLXXI, which, besides the XL Homilies of Saint Gregory, much at variance with the edition of the famous Maurist Fathers, has a calendar at the beginning, though missing three months; and the DCCXX, in which Saint Augustine's book *de quantitate animae* <gloss>on the quantity of the soul</gloss> is transcribed. In the ninth century, the lives of the saints are copied, which are described in the MXXV Codex, quite beautiful and ornate. This codex would deserve to be seen by the Bollandist Fathers.

From this foundation, therefore, has emerged the preparation of this Lamp or light, which, once ignited, burns continuously as long as the man from whose blood it is prepared draws vital breath <note>original: "vitalem ducit Spiritum", the Latin idiom for "is alive, breathes"</note>; and at the same hour, moment, or point that he breathes his last, it is extinguished together with him. Know furthermore: if the flame is bright, elevated, tranquil, and motionless, that man feels nothing that is heavy or burdensome to body or mind. But if it is otherwise, and the rising flame scintillates in various ways, or is lower, or cloudy and sluggish, let it be to you an indication of anxiety, sadness, and other Pathemata <note>passions or affections of the soul</note>. For, perpetually from the innate astral influences of the Microcosm and natural inclinations (since both that blood is nourished from the blood of the man himself, and his body from the substance of this very blood, from which the blood was, as it were, borrowed to prepare the Lamp), that flame shines out and shows itself according to the state and habit of that man, whether prosperous or adverse.

forever and always. But we also cannot deny that he allows the persecution of his Church to test his elect for as long as it pleases him; this is in no way for us to fathom or criticize.

For as God is, so also must all those be who wish to be his servants—though not in all things, but according to his commandments and holy will: pure, clear, chaste, simple, pious, patient, holy, and just. For how can one show the way to salvation who does not walk it himself, but walks another? How can one teach rightly who denies such teaching with his own life? Although Christ commanded that one should follow what those say who sit in the <term>Stuhl Moysis</term> <gloss>Chair of Moses</gloss>, and not what they do. Yet, the indicated saying is to be directed such that the office of the scribes of that time, though not to be despised, did not earn them praise. Rather, because of the offense they gave and especially because of their contempt for Christ, they could not escape temporal and eternal punishment afterward. And at that time, before the total destruction of the Jewish Kingdom, the <term>Saducæer</term> <gloss>Sadducees</gloss> and <term>Esseer</term> <gloss>Essenes</gloss> had separated themselves from the <term>Pharisæern</term> <gloss>Pharisees</gloss> and raised sects in teaching, which afterwards taught factions in the <term>republic</term> <gloss>state</gloss>. Yet, all at once, under and through the just judgment of God, their blood came upon them and their children.

<margin>It is shameful for a teacher when his own fault refutes him. <note>original: "Turpe est Doctori, cum culpa redarguit ipsum."</note></margin>

<margin>Even the smallest things seem prefigured to be fulfilled in the New Testament. <note>original: "Minima etiã præfigurata videntur. Impleri in Nouo Testamento."</note></margin>
Thus, some wish to apply the comparison now in these last times of the world as well, as if the Roman teachers are also surrounded by and dealing with the sects of the <term>Lutheraner</term> <gloss>Lutherans</gloss> and <term>Caluinisten</term> <gloss>Calvinists</gloss>. Because of their excesses, they are plagued by their own disciples and wayward monastics. Everything offensive and abusive is being removed, and such things, together with the sectarians and persecutors, shall be laid aside and abolished. The Church, however, shall be cleansed in this manner and led through the <term>Probfewr</term> <gloss>trial by fire</gloss>. Trusting in Christ her Bridegroom and his promise, she shall be possessed and ruled by him until the end; of this there is no doubt at all.

<margin>Actual repentance is another; that is, it is in place of baptism, or a new birth and regeneration. <note>original: "Pœnitentia actualis est alter: hoc est vice baptismus, seu noua, & regeneratio."</note></margin>

...where feet agree in a simple to double ratio, I pronounce the verse, I do not offend the judgment of your sense with any deceit. And yet that sound which is produced by shorter and, as it were, more fleeting syllables cannot occupy more time than it sounds. But if those judicial numbers were held by the bond of time in as much space as these sounding ones are arranged, they would not be able to attain the judgment of those sounding ones which are produced a little more lengthily by the same iambic law. Therefore, the delay of times does not hold those (numbers) which preside over judging. But if they were held by nothing, however much more lengthily I might utter sounds in iambic rhythm with suitable and mutually corresponding intervals, nevertheless they would be used for judging. But now, if I were to utter one syllable with the delay (not to say much) of three steps of someone walking, and another (syllable) with double (that delay), and thus in sequence I were to arrange such long iambs of simple and double (ratios), that law would nevertheless be preserved; yet we would not be able to apply that natural judgment to approving these dimensions. Therefore, those judicial (numbers) are also held by certain limits of temporal spaces, which they cannot exceed in judging; and whatever exceeds these spaces, they do not attain so as to judge. Yet these temper individual actions. For that which restrains and checks us in any attention of doing something with the limbs of the body from unequal movements – whether walking with unequal steps, or striking with unequal intervals of blows, or eating with unequal movements of the jaws, and finally scratching with unequal movements of the nails – and tacitly commands a certain equality, that very thing is a certain judicial something, which causes humans to have a sense and appreciation of beauty and decorum more than beasts, who rush to any of their impulses for the sake of appeasing bodily passion, and are not attracted by the grace and desire for beauty. [...removed from] fear, it is not ill-suited in any part if it is understood as referring to **Sarah**, the wife of **Abraham**, since the dates of the deceased **Hermes**—that is, **Canaan**, the grandson of **Noah**—and **Sarah** coincide, and the location (the city of **Hebron**, built by the **Canaanites**, or by **Heth**, the son of **Hermes**, where **Abraham** had established his residence) is most appropriate for the matter. <note>Borch is navigating a common 17th-century theory that merged biblical genealogy with alchemical history, identifying Hermes with the biblical Canaan to prove the "Art" was known to the Patriarchs.</note> Nor would it be unusual if **Hermes** had left traces of the **Art** <term>Art: The Great Art of Alchemy, encompassing the transmutation of metals and the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone.</term> in Egyptian caves, marked with hieroglyphic signs, and furthermore, that he intended his most noble discovery to be placed at his own tomb. Indeed, **Archimedes** once had the same plan; not content with leaving his discoveries to the pen, he also ordered that a sphere and a cylinder be placed upon his tomb as the glory of his invention, about which **Cicero** writes eloquently. <note>Cicero recounts in his *Tusculan Disputations* how he discovered Archimedes' neglected tomb in Syracuse by looking for these geometric symbols.</note> Meanwhile, I must not conceal that I have not yet found the *Emerald Tablet* among the Greek chemical writers, although I do not doubt it was regarded by them and passed down to the Latins. But truly, who has searched through all the Greek chemical manuscripts? Unless you prefer to agree with **Gaulmin** <note>Gilbert Gaulmin (1585–1665) was a French scholar who suggested that many Hermetic texts survived in Persian and Arabic before reaching Europe.</note> that the Tablet was found by the Persian victors either in Egypt or nearby, and was translated into Persian long ago, so that its name was unknown to the Greeks for a long time. However, in succeeding centuries, **Aristotle the Younger** <note>A pseudonym used by alchemical authors to borrow the authority of the Great Philosopher.</note> mentions the same tablet in his work *On the Perfect Mastery*; it is also mentioned by **Senior Zadith**, **Master Ortholanus** (or **Hortulanus**), **Avicenna**, **Arnald of Villanova**, **Isaac Hollandus**, **Albertus Magnus**, **Bernard of Trevisan**, and in the year of Christ 1330, **Petrus Bonus of Lombardy**, to say nothing of the almost infinite later writers. Let **Kircher** consider this, who contends that it was first shown to the world by the "Alchemist Canesius."

According to one account, the messenger mentioned above was Naritomi Hyōgo, though some also say it was Kuboshiro Kuboshi.

Regarding the instruction that descendants should not study military tactics: When one faces the battlefield, the power of discernment emerges, and it is something that cannot be stopped by any means. If you are governed by analytical thinking, you will be unable to break through enemy lines. A lack of calculation is essential when standing before the jaws of a tiger. If you have been listening to theories of military tactics, you will be filled with doubts, and you will never reach a resolution. It is said that he commanded his descendants not to study the practice of military tactics.

A certain general once said that for samurai other than the troop commanders, when testing armor, one should only test the front. Furthermore, he noted that the cords of the armor do not require special care, but the helmet must be inspected thoroughly. It is something one carries toward the enemy camp, after all, when taking a head.

Those who appear calm at the moment of death are suspicious. There are many such examples. It is understood that if a man who habitually talks a great deal becomes flustered at the moment of his death, he is not a true warrior.

When the Taikō Toyotomi Hideyoshi was a man of low standing, his companions left him behind. However, after he became the ruler of Japan, he spent every night writing out the administration of the realm and the allocation of stipends for his retainers.

In the <term>Enzan Hōgo</term> <gloss>Dharma words from Salt Mountain</gloss>, it is written: From a young age, a single doubt arose within me. If I were to inquire, "Who is the one who answers when I ask who it is that has achieved this personhood?" From the moment that singular doubt began, it grew deeper as the years passed. When I decided to enter the priesthood, a great vow arose. If I am to become a monk, I shall not seek the Way for my own sake alone. I shall attain the great law of the Buddhas, save all sentient beings, and only then seek complete enlightenment. Furthermore, until this doubt is resolved, I shall not study Buddhist teachings, nor shall I learn the etiquette of the clergy. If I must mingle with people, I shall place myself only among the wise teachers or in the mountains. After becoming a monk, as my doubt grew deeper, this vow also intensified. In the interval between the previous Buddha who has already attained nirvana and the future Buddha who has yet to appear in this world, at a time when the Buddhist law is fading, I wish to manifest a great path that will be an obstacle-free guide for the beings of this Buddha-less world. Even if I were to fall into the Avīchi hell <note>the lowest, most painful level of hell</note> because of the sin of this attachment, if I could only take the place of the suffering of sentient beings, I would never retreat.
